speaker: maya
text: Last time: Potosí, the silver mountain that bankrolled an empire. All of it ran on one thing: workers. And Spain kept running out of them. Four boxes on your sheet: the encomienda, the repartimiento, the Middle Passage, and the casta system with the hacienda hiding behind it. Circle the ones you couldn't explain right now. Twelve minutes, and you'll check all four off.

speaker: maya
text: Warm-up. Name every labor system the Spanish tried.

speaker: jay
text: Uh. Encomienda. Slavery. The... mita?

speaker: maya
text: Four, minimum. And the mita's Peru's, the same one-in-seven draft you locked last time. The deep question: what was the encomienda?

speaker: jay
text: The crown gives a colonist a bunch of Native people?

speaker: maya
text: Close. The crown granted a colonist the labor and tribute of a Native town. Not the land, the people. The colonist gets the work and owes the town protection and Christian teaching in return.

speaker: jay
text: So it's slavery with homework.

speaker: maya
text: Slavery with paperwork — and the paperwork mattered to the crown. Legally these were free subjects of the king. In practice the work quotas were brutal and the protection was mostly theoretical. Then the system started eating itself.

speaker: jay
text: How does a system eat itself?

speaker: maya
text: Disease kept emptying the towns. Between half and nine in ten Native people died between 1500 and 1650, so every grant shrank while the mines and plantations wanted more hands. A machine with no parts left.

speaker: maya
text: Somebody tried to fix it. Bartolomé de Las Casas, and he'd held an encomienda himself. Gave it back in 1514, in a sermon, and spent the next fifty years lobbying the crown. His big win came in 1542: the New Laws.

speaker: jay
text: What did the new laws say?

speaker: maya
text: Two things that matter. The encomienda dies with its holder: no passing it to your kids, the grant goes back to the crown. And no more forced personal service. Las Casas had read his Short Account to the court, and the court was horrified enough to act.

speaker: maya
text: Your turn. You're an encomendero in Peru, 1544. Your whole fortune is a grant that dies with you now. Your kids get nothing. What do you do?

speaker: maya
text: You fight. Gonzalo Pizarro raised an army of encomenderos. The crown sent its first viceroy of Peru, Blasco Núñez Vela, to enforce the laws. Pizarro's rebels met him at Añaquito in January 1546, and killed the king's viceroy on the field.

speaker: jay
text: They killed the viceroy. The king's guy.

speaker: maya
text: The king's guy, dead. And here's the question nobody can fully answer: if the crown had held its nerve, would the New Laws have worked? We'll never know. The crown blinked. It dropped the inheritance ban, and the encomenderos kept their grants.

speaker: jay
text: So the whole fix failed.

speaker: maya
text: The fix failed, and the crown learned the lesson: it stopped trying to kill the grant and started taking the assigning power instead. The trap on box one: the New Laws killed the encomienda. They didn't — the encomenderos killed the reform, and the viceroy.

speaker: maya
text: One down. Checking that one.

speaker: maya
text: Box two: the repartimiento. The crown's answer to the dead-viceroy problem.

speaker: jay
text: The answer was what, exactly?

speaker: maya
text: Take the assigning power away from the encomenderos and keep it. Native towns owed a rotating share of workers, and a crown official assigned them to settlers for short stints: farms, mines, workshops. Your turn ends, you go home.

speaker: jay
text: A draft. Like names out of a hat.

speaker: maya
text: A draft is exactly right. Repartimiento, from repartir, to divide up. The crown decided the encomenderos couldn't be trusted with the dividing, so it did the dividing itself. By 1549 the reforms were replacing the encomienda, and by 1550 the old system was done.

speaker: jay
text: Was the draft actually better?

speaker: maya
text: On paper: no more outright Indian slavery, and the workers were supposed to be paid wages. In practice? The empire stayed brutal. The crown just ran the operation more directly. That was the real change.

speaker: maya
text: And don't mix up the drafts: repartimiento is New Spain's, the mita is Peru's. Same idea, two names. If a question hands you Potosí, the answer's the mita.

speaker: jay
text: Repartimiento here, mita there. Got it.

speaker: maya
text: Box three: the Middle Passage. And it starts with a math problem.

speaker: jay
text: The towns just keep emptying.

speaker: maya
text: Between half and nine in ten Native people died between 1500 and 1650, mostly disease, though the wars and the work helped. Every draft, every grant kept shrinking. Meanwhile the silver still had to come out and the sugar still had to get cut.

speaker: maya
text: Your turn. The workers keep dying, the work doesn't shrink, and you need a workforce that won't run out. Where do you look?

speaker: maya
text: Across the ocean. The Portuguese had already built the machine: sugar plantations on the Atlantic islands, running on enslaved African labor, São Tomé was the model. Spain scaled it up to the Americas.

speaker: jay
text: "No matter how many died." Say the number.

speaker: maya
text: About thirteen out of every hundred died crossing. Roughly one in eight. Weeks below decks, in chains, with barely room to turn over. And the ships kept sailing anyway. The dying was priced in.

speaker: jay
text: They priced the dying in. Cold.

speaker: maya
text: I used to play hide-and-seek where I'd squeeze into the hall closet and stay too long. Dark, coats everywhere, couldn't move. That was a game. Now make it weeks, in the dark, in chains, and nobody's coming to find you.

speaker: jay
text: Okay. That's going to stick.

speaker: maya
text: One more thread, and it's Las Casas again. Early on, in a 1516 plan for fixing the Indies, he suggested bringing in enslaved Africans instead of working Natives to death.

speaker: jay
text: So the great defender of the Indians helped start the African slave trade.

speaker: maya
text: He didn't start it. Enslaved Africans were already being shipped before his proposal. What he did was lend it respectability. And decades later, in his History of the Indies, he took it back. Wrote that enslaving Africans was every bit as unjust, and he wasn't sure his good intentions would excuse him.

speaker: jay
text: An apology in a book nobody read for a century. Convenient.

speaker: maya
text: Partly convenient. But he came to believe both were wrong. Box three's common mistake: don't write that Las Casas invented the slave trade. He blessed it, then spent decades trying to un-bless it.

speaker: maya
text: Last box. The casta system. And it's not a labor system. It's what the labor systems built.

speaker: jay
text: A ladder, not a system?

speaker: maya
text: A ladder with legal teeth. Peninsulares at the top, Spaniards born in the Americas. Then criollos, Spaniards born in Spain. Below them the mestizos, then the mulatos, then Indigenous peoples and Africans at the bottom.

speaker: jay
text: Wait — you just said peninsulares were born in the Americas.

speaker: maya
text: Did I? ...I absolutely said the wrong one. Peninsulares: born in Spain. Criollos: born here. If I can mix those up mid-sentence, you can mix them up on the test, so nail it now.

speaker: jay
text: Peninsulares Spain, criollos Americas. Got it.

speaker: maya
text: The system was part custom, part law. Your label decided who paid tribute and who could hold office. The famous painting series ran through the combinations, every mixture named and ranked. An empire terrified of mixture, trying to write race into law.

speaker: jay
text: So where do the workers live in all this? The ladder's not a job.

speaker: maya
text: By the 1600s, on the hacienda. Big estates. And the flip: no grant of people this time. The power was the land itself.

speaker: jay
text: So who actually works it?

speaker: maya
text: Peons. Technically free workers, and that's the exam trap. The chain was debt. They got paid barely enough to live on, then took credit for everything else they needed, against the promise of future work. The debt never cleared, so the labor never left. The books call it debt peonage, and it looked a lot like serfdom.

speaker: jay
text: Peon. Like the little worker guys in Warcraft?

speaker: maya
text: Same word. Work work.

speaker: jay
text: Noted. Forever.

speaker: maya
text: Last box, last trap: don't write that peons were slaves. Free on paper, bound by the ledger. The debt was the chain.

speaker: maya
text: Lightning round. Four systems, one hunger. I name the trigger, you answer.

speaker: maya
text: The crown grants a colonist a town's labor.

speaker: jay
text: Encomienda. The grant.

speaker: maya
text: The crown takes the assigning power back.

speaker: jay
text: Repartimiento. The draft.

speaker: maya
text: The towns keep emptying, so Spain looks across the ocean.

speaker: jay
text: Enslaved African labor. The Middle Passage.

speaker: maya
text: The legal ladder, and the estates where the debt never clears.

speaker: jay
text: The casta system. And the hacienda.

speaker: maya
text: All four systems covered. Now let's see what stuck.

speaker: maya
text: Four boxes, let's land them. One: the encomienda. The crown grants a colonist a town's labor and tribute. Labor and tribute — not the land itself. The New Laws of 1542 tried to kill the inheritance; the encomenderos killed the viceroy instead, and the crown backed down.

speaker: jay
text: The grant, then the fight. Checked and filed.

speaker: maya
text: Two: the repartimiento. The crown takes the assigning power and runs a rotating draft: short stints, wages by the book, brutal anyway. Took over in fifteen... forty-nine?

speaker: jay
text: 1549. The crown does the dividing itself now.

speaker: jay
text: The draft, not the grant. Checked.

speaker: maya
text: Three: the Middle Passage. The Native workforce collapses, Spain turns to enslaved African labor on the Portuguese model. About one in eight died crossing, and Las Casas blessed it in 1516, then took it back.

speaker: jay
text: The crossing and the apology. Banked.

speaker: maya
text: Four: the casta ladder and the hacienda. Peninsulares, criollos, mestizos, mulatos, part custom, part law. And the estates, where debt did what chains used to do.

speaker: jay
text: The ladder and the ledger. All four checked.

speaker: maya
text: Three questions, AP-shaped. Say your answer before I give it.

speaker: maya
text: One, and it comes with a source. A ship's log from an Atlantic crossing lists four hundred captives boarded and three hundred forty-eight landed. A historian cites this log to make one point about the Middle Passage. What's the point?

speaker: maya
text: The dying was built into the business. Fifty-two of four hundred died, about thirteen percent, right on the average. The traders sailed anyway. The ships kept coming, so the trade kept working. The mortality didn't stop it, because it was expected.

speaker: maya
text: Two. The crown passed the New Laws in 1542. By the end of the decade the inheritance ban was dead. Why did the crown back down?

speaker: maya
text: The encomenderos rebelled, and the crown chose Peru over the reform. Gonzalo Pizarro raised an army, and the king's own viceroy was killed at Añaquito in 1546. Enforcing the laws cost a viceroy's life, so the crown dropped the ban and kept the colony.

speaker: maya
text: Three. A 1560s record shows a crown official assigning village workers to a silver mine for one month, then sending them home. Encomienda or repartimiento, and what detail decides it?

speaker: maya
text: Repartimiento. A crown official does the assigning, and the workers go home after a month. The encomienda handed a colonist the town's labor outright — the draft is the crown renting it by rotation.

speaker: maya
text: One more, fast. A peon owes the hacienda a debt he can never repay. Slave or free?

speaker: maya
text: Free, technically. The debt's the chain.

speaker: maya
text: Check your four boxes. Next time: 1550. Two scholars, one question: are the Native peoples of the Americas fully human, with rights, or natural slaves? The Valladolid debate.

speaker: maya
text: Four systems, one hunger —

speaker: jay
text: and the workers paid for all of them.
